My view on Confederate secession is usually unpopular in the circles I associate with. A lot of people that are Southern sympathizers though seem to want Catalans crushed because of their left leaning views.

Then there are many libertarians that favor secession and self-determination in principle. Personally I find these no less simplistic.

The question of whether secession is desirable I suppose it contingent on the individual cases and what the goals are. I can favor keeping the US intact but favor breaking up Russia or China. The motives should seem obvious. In some cases a break up or separation can also be conducted relatively straightforwardly with no thorny complications involving the viability of the state one secedes from being under threat. Spain and the US are and were seriously threatened by serious secession movements. The integrity of the Russian state though was not fundamentally threatened by the USSR breaking up.

The issues of justice and influence on foreign countries play some role too. Authoritarian states can be easier to break from. Divided populations like in Catalonia can make secession less compelling. And the fear of foreign states that the fever will spread to them is also a factor.

Then ultimately there is the matter of brute force. Whether the South had a 'right' to secede was settled at Appomattox. They didn't.

I identify loosely as libertarian (although the party itself doesn't generally stand for personal liberty and spends most of its time arguing about what color blue should be on the flag).

But I have to say I disagree with virtually everything you said here. While dismissing authoritarian states as undesirable you then seem to say that unlimited violence, the irreducible definition of authoritarianism, is acceptable, desirable even, if the "integrity" of the authoritarian regime is threatened. This statement should be in the examples section of the dictionary under Cognitive Dissonance.

One man's ideal society is another man's gulag. Self determination is ALWAYS the moral answer. And morals NEVER come with Buts; Limitations; Exceptions; or Footnotes.

If you want to discuss whether Catalonia can become a viable state that is a very different economic and military discussion that starts with what it means to be in the EU and ends with how one organizes their society. I will offer that I think it is probably a net negative for Catalonia, and as you tacitly acknowledge the loss of a huge cash cow for Spain to pay for their failing socialist state. It is quite obvious why the two sides hold the opinions they do. But if we go with the immutable Right of man to make his own decisions, even the really stupid ones, then the answer becomes obvious.

THE problem; the one that has plagued mankind since the dawn of history, is that a person in power views people not in power as useful cogs to accomplish HIS goals. If they can eek out happiness or fulfillment before they die that's a bonus. But not strictly speaking necessary. And too much happiness is probably not even desirable to the leader. If people are too happy they may question why they need his worthless ass in the first place.

An authoritarian state itself can be desirable or not depending on the specific circumstances in history in which it exists and what challenges are faced. My intent was not to dismiss authoritarian states but to allude to the fact that as they are usually seen in the West as having less legitimacy they can be easier to break away from. The authoritarian state often succumbs from exhaustion.

But democratic states that see a need to preserve territorial integrity for whatever reason are not in any meaningful sense authoritarian. They still retain a rights based and popular sovereignty based process by which to arrive at decisions. In my experience libertarians pretty much define as authoritarian whatever degree of government force they dislike. But it is a phony argument.
